1:
After the three days' fast the queen makes her venture, and the witnesses gather first around the timing and the royal robes she puts on. The reformed John Gill reckons this the third day of the fast Esther had appointed, noting that one Targum paraphrases it as the third day of the passover, the sixteenth of Nisan, and that the Jews came to fix the fast of Esther on the thirteenth of Adar. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agree without hesitation that it is the third day of the fast prescribed to Mordecai and the Jews in Esther 4:16; Ellicott adds that the words rendered "royal apparel" are literally "royalty," the queen clothing herself in the very insignia of her station.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the stage with care: on the third day Esther put on her royal apparel and stood in the inner court of the king's house, over against the dwelling where Ahasuerus sat upon his throne, facing the gate of the house. The whole chapter, they observe, turns on this approach and its sequel — the banquet she will spread, and the rage that will presently drive Haman home to raise a gallows.

But it is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who dwells longest on the courage of the moment. When the appointed time of fasting was finished, he says, Esther lost no time, but on the third day, while the impression of her devotions was fresh upon her spirit, she addressed herself to the king; for when the heart is enlarged in communion with God it is emboldened in doing and suffering for him. Resolutions that have difficulties and dangers to break through, he counsels, should be pursued without delay, lest they cool and slacken — what must be done boldly should be done quickly. Some think the three days' fast was but one whole day and two nights, reckoned three days as Christ's lying in the grave is so reckoned, which would suit the queen's appearing on the third day. Now she laid aside her fast-day garments and put on her robes of state, not to please herself but her husband; and Henry recalls her own words in the apocryphal supplement, that she abhorred the sign of her high estate and wore it only as she must. Let those whose rank obliges them to rich clothing, he adds, learn from her to be dead to it and not make it their adorning. So she stood in the inner court, over against the king, expecting her doom between hope and fear.
2:
The peril of the unbidden approach and its sudden reversal occupy the witnesses here. The reformed John Gill marks how much hung on the moment: the king had not called for Esther these thirty days and more, a coldness that gave her no assurance, and by coming uncalled she transgressed a law that might well have provoked his wrath — for a lesser matter than this Vashti had been divorced. Yet his mind was inclined to her, and she appeared amiable and pleasing in his eyes; and this, Gill insists, was of God, who holds the hearts of kings in his hand and turns them as he will. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the act itself: when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court she obtained favour in his sight, and he held out to her the golden sceptre in his hand; she drew near and touched its top — probably, they add with the Vulgate, kissed it.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the scene from the Greek. Adam Clarke relays the Septuagint's fuller account, in which the king at first looked upon her in kindled anger that she should appear unsummoned, so that she turned pale and fainted; whereupon God changed his spirit, and, touched with tenderness, he sprang from his throne, took her in his arms, and laid the golden sceptre upon her neck with endearing words. Clarke will not let the sceptre pass without its lesson, quoting Xenophon's Cyrus to his son: it is not the golden sceptre that saves the kingdom, but faithful friends are a king's truest and safest sceptre. John Wesley reads the two gestures as a silent exchange — the king held out the sceptre in testimony that he pardoned her presumption and stood ready to grant her petition, and she touched its top in token of her thankful acceptance, her reverence, and her submission.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the rescue. The king protected her from the law and assured her of safety by holding out the golden sceptre, which she thankfully touched, presenting herself as a humble petitioner; and having had power with God and prevailed, like Jacob at Peniel, she now had power with men as well. He that will lose his life for God, Henry adds, shall save it, or find it in a better life. The witnesses do not divide: the favour was real, but it was God's own doing, the turning of a despot's heart at the very instant a law stood ready to condemn.
3:
No sooner is she safe than the king presses her with an open-handed question, and the witnesses weigh both his readiness and the vastness of his offer. The reformed John Gill takes it simply: the king supposed she had come upon some business, some suit to lay before him, and so invited it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same inference more fully — concluding from her unsummoned appearance that some urgent matter pressed her, he said, "What wilt thou, Queen Esther? and what is thy request? To the half of the kingdom it shall be granted thee," a compressed way of promising that even were her request to reach half his realm, it should be given.

Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, hears in that promise a royal extravagance that recurs across the book, renewed at the banquet in v.6 and again in Esther 7:2; and he notes that the very same reckless words would fall from Herod Antipas to the daughter of Herodias in Mark 6:23. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the offer as proverbial — "to the half of the kingdom" meaning that nothing in reason should be denied her — and finds in the king's "it shall be given" a token of how God in his providence often prevents the fears and outdoes the hopes of his servants.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the whole exchange into an encouragement to prayer. So far was the king from counting her an offender, he observes, that he seemed glad to see her and eager to oblige; he that had divorced one wife for not coming when she was sent for would not be severe to another for coming when she was not sent for. Esther had feared she would perish, and instead was promised whatever she might ask, though it were half the kingdom — for God can turn the hearts of great men, even those who act most arbitrarily, which way he pleases. Henry draws the lesson our Saviour draws from the parable of the importunate widow in Luke 18:6-8: if this proud and imperious king could say to the queen, "What is thy petition? it shall be granted," shall not God hear and answer the prayers of his own elect who cry to him day and night? Esther came to a haughty man with a law against her and an enemy at the king's right hand; believers come to a God of love and grace, invited, with a promise in their favour and an Advocate with the Father. Let us therefore, Henry urges, come boldly to the throne of grace.
4:
Given leave to ask anything, Esther asks only that the king and Haman come to a banquet she has prepared, and the witnesses read the modest request as a piece of careful strategy. The reformed John Gill notes that she humbly submits the matter to the king's pleasure, intimating only how welcome his coming would be to her. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the plain sense — she requested that on that very day the king and Haman come to the banquet she had made, her courteous "if it seem good unto the king" echoing the formula of Esther 1:19 — and observe that she invited Haman deliberately, that (as Calovius put it) she might accuse him to his face in the king's presence and cut off every avenue of evasion.

Charles Ellicott, reading as a grammatical-historical witness, finds in her hesitation the mark of how much hung upon the request. With so great a matter at stake, and for all the king's promise still uneasy in her mind, she temporises; she gains time, and she secures a specially favourable moment for bringing her petition forward — and the king perceives that she is holding her real request in reserve, since he must ask again. Ellicott catches a fine grammatical shift that tracks her boldness: so long as she is working her way up to firm ground she speaks of the king in the third person, "let the king come," but when at last she makes her decisive appeal she turns to the second, "in thy sight, O king."

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh why Haman was included. Adam Clarke judges it necessary to invite him precisely to prevent his suspicion, lest he take some hasty step that might frustrate the great design now forming. John Wesley reads it as courtesy turned to advantage: by showing such respect to the king's chief favourite she might insinuate herself the more into the king's affection, and so, when she saw fit, present her petition with the better hope. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the queen's several aims into one design of prudence — to signify how much she valued the king's favour and company, to try how he stood affected toward her, to soften his spirit that he might more tenderly receive her complaint, to please him by her deference to Haman, and to gain at the banquet of wine a fairer opportunity to plead. Wisdom, Henry remarks, is profitable to direct; some men are hard to deal with, and must be taken by the right handle.
5:
The king's answer is a single brisk command, and the witnesses, few here, hear in it both his eagerness and a darker undertone he cannot see. The reformed John Gill explains the order simply: the king bade some of his servants make haste and acquaint Haman with the queen's invitation, pressing him to comply without delay — for Haman was too great a man to be kept waiting, and the honour of the queen's table was one the king would not have him miss. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the Hebrew: "cause Haman to make haste" means the king sent to fetch him quickly, that the word of the queen might be carried out; the verb, they observe, is the same brisk "hasten" used when Ahab's servant is sent to fetch Micaiah in 1 Kings 22:9 and 2 Chron. 18:8; and so, they note, the king and Haman came together to the banquet Esther had prepared.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the king's readiness as a sign of the affection he still bore his queen. That he came at once, and ordered Haman to come along with him, was an indication of the kindness he yet retained for her; had he really designed the destruction of Esther and her people, Henry reasons, he would never have accepted her banquet. The ease of his compliance is thus quietly reassuring — the decree against the Jews, sealed with his own ring, had been Haman's contrivance rather than the king's own settled hatred, and here the king moves gladly toward the very woman whose nation that decree condemned; and in that ready compliance the queen might read a first token that her petition would not in the end be refused.

Yet the witnesses let the reader feel what the actors cannot. The king summons Haman to the feast in all good humour, and Haman hastens to it flattered and unsuspecting; neither knows that the banquet Esther has spread is to be the appointed place of the favourite's undoing. The invitation so graciously pressed and so gladly answered is gathering Haman to a table where his own accusation waits. There is a grim providence in the very haste the king commands: the man is hurried toward his ruin, and the promptness that seems to crown his fortunes is speeding him to the hour when they will be reversed. So the witnesses, without straining the plain words, mark how a small domestic scene — a king pleased, a servant sent, a favourite fetched in haste — is made the hinge of a far greater deliverance than any at the table yet suspects.
6:
At the banquet the king renews his question over the wine, and the witnesses pause to describe the setting before they weigh the words. The reformed John Gill explains that this was properly a "banquet of wine" — not a meal of meats, dinner or supper, but the drinking that followed; the Persians, he notes from Aelian, took their food in two courses, the first of meats with water, the second of fruits with wine, and it was over this second course, when the king had begun to be cheerful, that he accosted the queen — for the Persians, Gill reports from Aelian, when they had eaten their fill, gave themselves to the drinking of wine. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that it was at the point of the feast when the wine was introduced, and John Wesley likewise: it was called the banquet of wine because it consisted not of meats, which the king had already eaten, but of fruits and wines, such entertainments being frequent among the Persians. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical witness, calls it the continuation of the banquet of v.5 — the dessert, so to speak.

His fellow grammatical-historical commentators Keil and Delitzsch fix on the moment and the promise. It was at the banquet of wine, when the greatest cheerfulness would prevail, that the king repeated his question about the queen's desire, renewing the same generous pledge he had made at the sceptre in v.3; the verb they render as an optative — "and it shall be done." The king, that is, does not wait for Esther to speak, but presses his offer a second time, in the mellowest hour of the feast.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the renewed enquiry the same open generosity he found at the throne. Here again the king asks, "What is thy petition? and it shall be granted, even to the half of the kingdom" — a proverbial largeness, Henry observes, by which he assured her he would deny her nothing in reason, the very phrase Herod would later use to the dancing girl in Mark 6:23. The witnesses do not divide. Together they show a king relaxed and expansive, twice pressing his queen to name her desire, all unaware that the request she is holding back concerns his own decree and the life of his favourite. Twice now the royal bounty has been laid before her, and twice she has held her peace, waiting for a surer hour; the cheerfulness of the wine is the very air in which, on the morrow, her terrible petition will fall.
7:
Esther begins to answer, and then draws back, and the witnesses attend to the pregnant pause. The reformed John Gill notes that she names "my petition and my request," but for wise reasons still defers the principal one she has to make, offering for the present only a lesser thing; for the moment she asks nothing but the king's company again, and Haman's, at a second feast of her own preparing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the broken sentence exactly: she opens, "My petition and my request —" and then stops, saying only that if the king will do her the favour of coming with Haman to a banquet on the morrow, she will then bring her petition forward. She did not judge the moment, in the midst of the gaiety, an appropriate one for laying it before him. And they mark again her deliberate reason for including Haman on both occasions — that, as Calovius observed, she might arraign him in the king's very presence, charging him with the decree he had stealthily obtained against her people, and shut against him every path of cavil and escape.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the wisdom of the delay. The adjourning of the main petition he ascribes first to Esther's prudence: thus she hoped yet further to win upon the king and ingratiate herself with him. Perhaps, he allows, her heart failed her now that she stood on the point of asking, and she desired more time for prayer, that God would give her a mouth and wisdom. The putting of it off, moreover, would be well taken as an expression of her deep reverence for the king and her unwillingness to press too hard upon him; for what is hastily asked, Henry remarks, is often as hastily denied, but what is asked with a pause deserves to be considered; and the delay, well managed, would only raise her petition in the king's esteem.

Yet Henry will not leave the delay to human calculation alone. Beyond Esther's prudence he sees the hand of God, putting it into her heart to defer her petition a day longer; she knew not why, but God did — that what was to fall out in the night between this banquet and the next might further her design and open her way to success. The witnesses converge on a single reading: the queen's reticence is at once a stroke of policy and a movement of providence, the reserve of a wise petitioner and the overruling of a God who is arranging, unseen, the very order of the days.
8:
Now Esther states her deferral outright, and the witnesses divide their attention over why she puts the great asking off until the morrow. The reformed John Gill reads the opening clause as a settled certainty rather than a doubt — "seeing I have found favour in the king's sight," a favour already proved by the golden sceptre held out to her and by his acceptance of her banquet. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the plain sense of the postponement: if it please the king, let him come with Haman to the banquet she will prepare, and "to-morrow I will do as the king hath said" — that is, make known her request.

But over the reason for the delay the emphases part. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses divide the motive between the queen's craft and something less composed. Adam Clarke thinks she saw she was gaining upon the king's affections but was not yet sufficiently confident, and so wished another interview to ingratiate herself more fully and make her success sure. John Wesley allows the same prudence — that she would further engage the king's affection, and intimate that her petition was of no ordinary kind — but adds that perhaps she was a little daunted in the king's presence, her courage of utterance failing her for the moment. Both, however, and Clarke expressly, subordinate every human reason to a higher one: Providence disposed things thus, taking away her courage this once, to give room for the great accident of the coming night. Clarke draws the point out plainly — things were so ordered to give time for the important event of the following chapter, on which the whole deliverance would presently turn. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same way — God put it into Esther's heart to delay a day longer; she knew not, but God knew, what was to happen that very night.

So the witnesses hold two accounts of the delay in a single hand. Some weight it as deliberate strategy — a queen choosing her ground, ingratiating herself, showing reverence; others confess a failure of nerve, courage that would not come. But all agree that beneath the prudence and the trembling alike ran the secret purpose of God, who meant the intervening night for a work none of them yet foresaw. The two readings are not finally at odds, for the daunted heart and the calculating mind may each be an instrument in a hand that governs them both. Whether Esther paused by policy or by faltering, the pause itself was of the Lord, and it made room for Mordecai's deliverance and Haman's fall.
9:
The scene shifts from the banquet to the gate, and the witnesses watch pride and rage collide in a single man. The reformed John Gill marks only that Haman went out from the court toward his own house joyful and glad of heart; the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add that his good humour lasted precisely until he saw Mordecai in the king's gate, who neither stood up nor trembled before him, so that he was filled with indignation — the Hebrew, they note, meaning that Mordecai did not so much as quake at his approach.

The deeper interest of the verse, for the witnesses, is Mordecai's refusal, and here they genuinely divide. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it as an act of faith: Mordecai neither rose nor moved, to show how little he feared Haman, and how firm was his confidence in his God, who would deliver him and his people in this great exigency. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it as conscience: Mordecai was as determined as ever, acting from a principle he would not betray even now that he had reason to fear; those who walk in holy sincerity may walk in holy security, for he that walks uprightly walks surely. But Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical witness, judges the refusal more harshly: in Esther 3:2 Mordecai had declined to bow or prostrate himself to Haman, which was honourable independence; here he refuses even the slightest sign of respect, and what was once integrity has, in Ellicott's eyes, become indefensible rudeness. Adam Clarke stands between them, granting that Mordecai carried his inflexibility to its highest pitch, yet supposing that some reverence was required which he could not conscientiously pay.

Henry alone lingers over what the affront did to Haman. He was full of indignation, and yet, as the next verse will tell, he refrained himself — a struggle in which his anger, which would gladly have run Mordecai through on the spot, wrestled with his malice, which had resolved to wait for the general massacre. This little slight, Henry says, was the dead fly that spoiled the whole pot of Haman's precious ointment; those disposed to be uneasy will never want something to be uneasy at, and proud men, though they have much to their mind, count it all as nothing if they have not everything to their mind. The witnesses leave the gate with the favourite's joy already soured, and a good man's quiet refusal exposing, as nothing else could, the bottomless discontent of pride.
10:
Haman masters himself for the moment, and the witnesses find in that restraint less a virtue than a calculation — and, beneath it, a providence. The reformed John Gill explains that Haman refrained from any open resentment or revenge upon Mordecai as being beneath him: he would not stoop to avenge himself on a single man, holding it too mean a thing for one of his greatness, when the whole people to whom Mordecai belonged would shortly feel the weight of his hand for the insolent treatment their kinsman had shown him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same self-command: without immediately venting his rage he went home and sent for his friends and his wife Zeresh, that he might unburden his galled spirit before them and take counsel with them for Mordecai's destruction.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley looks past Haman's motive to the hand that governed it. Haman could easily have taken present vengeance, by his own hand or his servants', without fear of any inconvenience to himself; that he did not was the work of God's wise and powerful providence, disposing Haman's heart against its own inclination and making him, as it were, fasten fetters upon his own hands. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same inward war: the indignation that demanded Mordecai's blood at once was held in check by the malice that had determined to wait for the appointed day, so that thorns and snares, in Solomon's phrase, were in the way of the froward.

Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, turns aside to the wife whom Haman now summons. Zeresh, he observes, is a name probably drawn from an old Persian word for "gold"; and according to the Targum she was the daughter of Tatnai, the governor beyond the river whose opposition to the returning exiles is recorded in Ezra 5:3. The witnesses do not divide. They show a proud man too vain to strike a lone Jew, hoarding his revenge for a national slaughter, gathering wife and friends to feed his wounded pride — and all the while, without knowing it, held back by a providence that meant the delay for his own destruction rather than Mordecai's. That a man so exalted must convene a council of wife and friends over the unbent neck of one doorkeeper is itself the measure of how deeply the slight had entered. The restraint Haman takes for his own dignity, Wesley says, was God's fetter upon his hands.
11:
Summoned to hear him, Haman's friends are treated first to an inventory of his greatness, and the witnesses read the recital as vanity feeding on itself. The reformed John Gill judges that Haman told them of the glory of his riches partly in ostentation, partly to ease his mind under the mortification Mordecai had given him, and chiefly to aggravate that affront — that a man of such wealth should be slighted by a single Jew. On the multitude of his children he notes that Haman had ten sons, though the former Targum absurdly swells the number beyond credit to two hundred and eight besides those ten, and that among the Persians a man rich in children was held in great esteem, the king sending yearly gifts to him who had the most. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the point from the historians: Haman first paraded his wealth and domestic felicity, the glory of his riches and the multitude of his children — ten sons, as Esther 9:7-10 records — many sons being reckoned a signal prosperity among the Persians, so that, Herodotus reports, the king sent presents each year to the man with the greatest number; then he rehearsed the honours the king had heaped on him, advancing him above all the princes and servants, as at Esther 3:1.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds a note on the children Haman prized so highly: the Asiatic sovereigns, and their great men after them, delighted in the number of their offspring, which was one reason they took so many wives and concubines. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical witness, hears in the whole speech nothing but empty boasting. All that Haman recounted was already well known to his hearers; to parade it thus was mere vain-glory — the pride, Ellicott says, that goeth before destruction.

The witnesses converge on a single portrait. Here is a man who has everything the world counts great — riches, a houseful of sons, promotion above every peer, the ear of the king — and who must yet summon his household to admire it, cataloguing his blessings aloud to a wife and friends who know them already. The catalogue is long, and every item in it true; what is false is only the peace that Haman imagines it should buy him. The very length of the boast betrays the wound beneath it; a felicity that must be rehearsed to be felt is a felicity already spoiled, and the reader is being prepared to hear, in the next breath, that all of it avails him nothing.
12:
To the catalogue of his greatness Haman adds the honour that pleases him most, and the witnesses see in it the height of his self-deception. The reformed John Gill notes that to all the rest he now joined what seemed to delight him above everything — a fresh and singular honour done to him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the boast in his own words: Queen Esther let no man come in with the king to the banquet she had prepared but himself, and on the morrow he is again invited to her table with the king. To be the sole guest of king and queen together, twice over, seemed to Haman the very pinnacle of his fortunes.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley catches the irony that hangs over the words. Here Haman makes a matter of glorying out of the very thing that would prove the occasion of his utter ruin; so ignorant are the wisest of men, Wesley reflects, and so liable to fatal mistakes, rejoicing in what they have most cause to fear. He glories, that is, in his own summons to judgment, mistaking the queen's snare for her singular favour. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry drives the point home. Haman valued himself on the invitation, and thought it brought him near to the perfection of felicity that the queen would admit no one but his mighty self to attend the king; he flattered himself that she meant thereby to honour him, whereas in truth she meant to accuse him, and in calling him to the banquet was calling him to the bar. Self-admirers and self-flatterers, Henry warns, are really self-deceivers; the pride of the heart deceives the proud, as in Obad. 3 — and he asks what magnifying glasses proud men look at their faces in, that they should so mistake a summons to judgment for a crowning grace. The higher a proud man is lifted, Henry observes, the further his folly overreaches, till he reads his very indictment as a compliment.

The witnesses do not divide. They gather around the same bitter comedy: the favourite recounting, as the crown of his good fortune, the two invitations that will destroy him, reading the queen's careful courtesy as homage to himself when it is the quiet closing of a snare. Esther's second banquet, which Haman parades before his friends as proof that none stands so high as he, is the very table at which his accusation waits; and the reader, who knows what Haman cannot, watches a proud man boast most loudly of the thing that will undo him.
13:
For all his greatness, one unbending Jew empties it of worth, and the witnesses make Haman's confession the text for a meditation on the restlessness of pride. The reformed John Gill hears in "yet all this availeth me nothing" a man for whom no abundance is sufficient: it gives him no satisfaction, no contentment. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the Hebrew closely — all this is "not equalled to me," does not answer my desires — the whole of his fortune failing to content him so often as he sees Mordecai the Jew sitting unmoved in the king's gate; and Charles Ellicott, their fellow grammatical-historical voice, sharpens the same verb: better than "availeth me nothing" is "suiteth me not," "contenteth me not."

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the confession into a lesson on the soul. John Wesley marvels that a man so favoured should be so tormented by his own envy and malice: though proud men have much to their mind, if they have not all to their mind it is nothing; the thousandth part of what Haman possessed would make a modest and humble man as happy as he could wish, yet Haman complains as passionately as though sunk into the lowest poverty. Adam Clarke turns the verse into a searching sermon. Pride, he says, ever renders its possessor unhappy, conceiving itself defrauded by every one who withholds the respect it claims; and the reason lies deeper still — the soul was made for God, and nothing but God can fill it or make it happy. So Solomon in all his glory found everything vanity and vexation because his soul had not God for its portion; so Ahab on his throne took to his bed and would not eat, wanting God in his heart; and so Haman, prime favourite of the king, is wretched because he cannot have a bow from a man his own heart despised. How wretched, Clarke concludes, is the man who has not the God of Jacob for his help, and in whose heart Christ dwells not by faith.

The witnesses do not divide. They read in one line the whole anatomy of a discontented greatness: honours without number, and not a moment's peace; a man master of an empire's second seat, undone by the unbowed head of a single doorkeeper. What Haman lacks is not another dignity but a heart at rest, and that no king can give him.
14:
The wounded favourite is given a remedy for his discontent, and the witnesses close the chapter on the gallows that his own household advises. The reformed John Gill supposes it was Zeresh his wife who first moved the counsel, with all his friends approving and uniting in it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the advice: let a tree fifty cubits high be set up, and on the morrow let Haman ask the king that Mordecai be hanged upon it — impaled, as the same word implies at Esther 2:23 — and then let him go merrily with the king to the banquet. The counsellors take it for granted the king will grant the request without hesitation; and the stake is made high, they note, that it may be seen the farther.

On the manner of the death the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agree, against the plain English "gallows." The Hebrew word, Clarke explains, means simply wood, a tree or pole, some seventy-five feet high, that Mordecai's shame might be the greater and his suffering the more public; and he takes it, like Ellicott, for impaling rather than hanging. Ellicott presses the philology: the word stands both for a living tree and for the artificial structure, hanging as we know it not being a Persian punishment, so that crucifixion is doubtless meant — the very word the Greek translators use here is that used in the New Testament for the cross of the Saviour, and the Latin renders it "crucem." Clarke recalls too that in later ages the Jews were wont to burn Haman in effigy, and with him a wooden cross said to commemorate the one he here raised for Mordecai — a custom the emperors Justinian and Theodosius abolished by their edicts. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds only that the great height was designed to make the spectacle conspicuous to all, the more to disgrace Mordecai and to strike Haman's enemies with a dread of despising or opposing him.

The witnesses do not divide, and the chapter ends where pride always tends. The thing pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made that very hour — a tree towering fifty cubits before his own door, prepared for a man who had done him no wrong but decline to bow. The instrument of another's shame, the witnesses let us see, is being shaped by the shamed man's own hands. He goes to his bed pleased with the thought of seeing Mordecai hanged in the morning and then feasting merrily with the king, not dreaming whose neck the timber he has raised is destined at last to bear.
